title: The Politics of Canada in the Shadow of Empire: a Q&A with Yves Engler
author: Daniel Falcone
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Donald_Trump_greets_Prime_Minister_of_Canada_Mark_Carney_Tuesday_May_6_2025_at_the_West_Wing_entrance_of_the_White_House-680x511.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/12/the-
politics-of-canada-in-the-shadow-of-empire-a-qa-with-yves-engler/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Donald_Trump_greets_Prime_Minister_of_Canada_Mark_Carney_Tuesday_May_6_2025_at_the_West_Wing_entrance_of_the_White_House-680x511.jpg)

Photograph Soruce: The White House - Public Domain

Canadian foreign policy is at times presented as rights-based and as an
example of textbook multilateralism. The _left often_ argues, however, that
beneath the surface lies a politics of power that aligns Ottawa’s interests
with the Pentagon’s. This raises questions about the country’s role in peace
and conflict. In this exclusive interview from Montreal for _CounterPunch_ ,
writer and activist [Yves Engler](https://yvesengler.com/), co-author of
[_Canada’s Long Fight Against
Democracy_](https://www.barakabooks.com/catalogue/canadas-long-fight-against-
democracy/)(Baraka Books, 2024), looks at the contradictions shaping Canada’s
global politics under Prime Minister Mark Carney. He covers Canada’s
relationship with the US and the overall limitations of Canadian sovereignty.
Further, Engler comments on the nation’s response to Gaza and the
unprecedented protest movements it has inspired across the country. He looks
at the future of Canadian Liberal foreign policy as the hemisphere tilts
closer towards [fascism](https://fpif.org/the-myth-of-a-global-antifa/).

_**Daniel Falcone:** You covered a lot regarding Canada’s foreign policy in
[The House of Mirrors: Justin Trudeau’s Foreign Policy
](https://www.palestinechronicle.com/house-of-mirrors-justin-trudeaus-foreign-
policy-book-review/)(Black Rose Books, 2020). In author Peter McFarlane’s
recent work, [Last Call for Canada: Sovereign Nation or Vassal State
](https://www.barakabooks.com/catalogue/last-call-canada/)(Baraka Books,
2026), he cites George Grant’s [Lament for a Nation: The Defeat of Canadian
Nationalism ](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.cttq474c)(McGill–Queen’s
University Press, 1965). Grant raised initial concerns about Canadian
sovereignty at the hands of US influence. How does Canada’s relationship with
the US impact its ability to pursue a “progressive” foreign policy in the Mark
Carney era, especially concerning the Middle East?_

**Yves Engler:** The elite in Canada see the world and profit from it in ways
that are very similar to the elite in the US. There is [opposition to
Trump](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-business-brief-
opposition-to-trump-grows-in-unexpected-places/) that can elicit a nationalist
backlash, so there is hostility in that sense. But if you look at the long-
term picture, at least [since World War
II](https://www.historymuseum.ca/blog/the-pattern-of-canada-us-relations) or
arguably going back [more than a century](https://www.cfr.org/articles/us-
canada-relations), there has been this basic view of the world organized
around profit that is remarkably similar on both sides of the border. You can
see that historically. For instance, when the [US occupied
Cuba](https://www.queensu.ca/cidp/sites/cidpwww/files/uploaded_files/Martello21.pdf),
the Royal Bank of Canada was the preferred bank because at that time there
were restrictions on the international operations of US banks. Thus the [Royal
Bank of Canada (RBC)](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/royal-
bank-of-canada), still Canada’s largest bank today, became the main financial
institution for the US occupation of Cuba. That is just one very concrete
example of Canadian capital benefiting from US imperial domination around the
world.

That must be a central part of the discussion. Obviously, you can point out
innumerable examples of it. [Carney](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/profile/mark-
carney/), I think, is somebody who just sees the world the way an
[international banker](https://nationalpost.com/opinion/carney-gets-a-little-
help-from-his-international-banking-friends) does. That is what he has been
for the better part of 30-plus years at Goldman Sachs, Brookfield Asset
Management, as governor of the Bank of Canada, and then governor of the Bank
of England. He sees the world through a certain Eurocentric capitalist lens.
But he is also a leader [boxed in by Canada’s relationship with the
US](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-canada-us-trade-deal-
deadline-carney-august-5-comments/). (See: recent US placement of heavy
tariffs, going up to 50%, on Canadian metals like aluminum; crude oil and
energy products are exempt from these threats). So then, the US relationship
obviously has an impact on whether the Carney government is going to oppose
the genocide in [Gaza](https://nationalpost.com/opinion/matthew-taub-a-year-
later-what-happened-to-carneys-conditions-for-recognizing-palestine) or
support Trump’s attack on
[Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93Iran_relations).

In the case of Iran, Carney came out almost immediately to endorse it. He
[later backed away](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c9q5pqyj5gwo)
rhetorically but his [initial
statement](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/statements/2026/02/28/statement-prime-
minister-carney-and-minister-anand-situation-middle-east) was supportive. More
important than the rhetoric, however, is that Canada has a base in
[Kuwait](https://globalnews.ca/news/11728266/iran-kuwait-military-base-canada-
attack/) located on a US base with about 200 Canadian troops stationed there.
Canada also has bases (“operational support hubs”) in
[Jamaica](https://nbmediacoop.org/2011/08/12/canadian-military-tests-its-new-
base-in-jamaica/), [Senegal](https://breachmedia.ca/canada-building-global-
network-of-military-bases-in-aggressive-shift/), and
[Germany](https://www.canada.ca/en/department-national-defence/services/bases-
support-units/canadian-forces-in-europe.html) that are explicitly part of
supporting the Pentagon’s global military infrastructure. There are also
recent reports that Canadian officers oversaw the US base in
[Qatar](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/iran-air-strikes-canada-israel-
war-9.7110268) from the middle of last year through the end of the year. When
Israel and the US attacked Iran during the [12-day
conflict](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/iran-air-strikes-canada-israel-
war-9.7110268), it was a Canadian overseeing air operations. These are all
parts of the uniquely close ties between the Canadian and US militaries. There
is no other military that is more integrated with the US military than
Canada’s, with hundreds of formal agreements between them.

Therefore, the Canadian military is very much structured to assist the US
military around the world. It is not structured to defend Canada against the
only country that could realistically invade it, which is of course the
[US](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/51-state-carney-trump-hoekstra-trade-
talks-9.7221755). The point is that there is a curtailment of [Canadian
sovereignty](https://cdhowe.org/publication/fortress-north-america-is-a-
threat-to-canadas-sovereignty/) in a fundamental sense [via Fortress North
America]. But Canada’s capitalist elite do not actually want sovereignty in
some ways. They want to be part of the US empire, just as they were once part
of the British Empire. Concretely, the Canadian military (and nationalism)
itself was created as an institution of the British Empire that conquered
these lands. Then, over the past seven decades, it has increasingly become a
[historical](https://journals.openedition.org/eccs/1279?lang=en) extension of
US empire.

_**Daniel Falcone:** Can you talk about the role of [Canadian civil
society](https://aidwatchcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/DFATD-CSO-
Policy.pdf) in global politics? What is their collective reaction to Canada’s
foreign policy in terms of upholding human rights and international law in
relation to [Gaza](https://www.globalsumudflotilla.org/delegations/canada/)? I
know that Doctors Without Borders, for example, has done great work on this.
(See: [Humanitarian Negotiations Revealed: The MSF Experience: A behind-the-
scenes account of MSF decision-making,
2012](https://evaluation.msf.org/evaluation-report/humanitarian-negotiations-
revealed-the-msf-experience))._

**Yves Engler:** Palestine is something unique because there has been a
substantive, organized protest movement. The movements against the Canadian
role in the genocide in Gaza are the most significant and sustained popular
uprisings against Canada’s complicity in international crimes. There really
hasn’t been anything else on this scale. There were major protests of
[apartheid in South
Africa](https://www.labourheritagecentre.ca/collection/b-c-unions-take-a-
stand-against-apartheid-in-south-africa/) that went on for a long time, but
they were nowhere near as significant as the protests we’ve seen over the past
three years. There were also big movements against Canada formally joining the
[Iraq War in 2003](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/canadians-join-global-peace-
rally-1.397326), and those were very sizable here in Montreal.

Although the protests to the Iraq War were larger than anything we’ve seen in
Gaza (the high point for Gaza was around 50,000 people, while for the Iraq War
we reached close to 100,000 people twice, for two different demonstrations),
the difference with Gaza is the sustained nature of the [social
movement](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yw13pS7qB7w).

Here in [Montreal](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/gaza-protest-
downtown-montreal-1.7561909) there were protests every weekend for two years.
There were many protests with 50,000 people, and then 10,000, 20,000, multiple
times. Even a year and a half into it, demonstrations were still regularly
drawing more than 1,000 people. Then it shifted with protests happening on
both Saturdays and Sundays, partly because of some internal divisions within
the movement. But there has never been a more [active street
movement](https://electronicintifada.net/content/montreal-provides-model-
student-activism/51374). I’ve been to around 250 Palestine-related
demonstrations and actions over the past three years myself.

It is contradictory in the sense that we still have not won the big, obvious
policy change that should have been the lowest-hanging fruit, a [formal arms
embargo](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/protest-arms-embargo-
repentigny-manufacturer-1.7615604). Looking back, the [Trudeau
government](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/arms-ammunition-shipments-israel-
canada-1.7596091) claimed that Canada was not selling weapons to Israel, and
that was mostly a lie. But even the limited measures they announced only
addressed a small part of Canadian arms exports, because the major channel is
through the US. Canada has a 60-year-old [Defense Production Sharing
Agreement](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/industry-sector-
intelligence/manufacturing-industries/aerospace-and-defence/defence-
development-sharing-agreement-between-canada-and-united-states-america) with
the US, where arms sales are not even fully tabulated in the same way.

For example, [General Dynamics](https://www.gdotscanada.com/) here in Montreal
were still sending things like components and small arms ammunition to Israel
throughout that period. The arms embargo that the government claimed to have
introduced, which was supposed to end permits for arms sales, wasn’t even
addressing most of the arms transfers that were happening through the US to
Israel. (Note: The current Canadian government claims that since January 8,
2024, it has not approved new permits for weapons that could be used in Gaza).

Overall, though, regarding Gaza, the large movement has had massive amounts of
protest activity, including the [encampment at
McGill](https://www.mcgilldaily.com/2024/08/unfolding-the-mcgill-encampment/),
which was very prominent. I was there for four months during the student
encampment. It featured many direct actions and all kinds of other organizing.
Similar versions of this happened across the country. We didn’t win in terms
of major policy changes but there have been some smaller wins and rhetorical
shifts from the government. For example, they began criticizing Israel more
openly and said that they would arrest
[Netanyahu](https://www.cija.ca/canada_obligated_under_international_law_to_arrest_netanyahu_if_he_enters_country_trudeau_citynews_toronto)
if he came to Canada, even though he has flown through [Canadian
airspace](https://justiceinconflict.org/2026/02/24/middle-power-problems-what-
if-canada-arrested-netanyahu-when-he-flew-over-its-provinces/) several times.

We also saw a major shift in public opinion, and it has changed very
significantly. All these protests have clearly chipped away, slowly, over time
at public perceptions of Israel and Zionism. There have been other major
movements re:
[Afghanistan](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/canada-and-the-
war-in-afghanistan-plain-language-summary) and historic movements around
nuclear weapons and the [Vietnam
War](https://www.mulroneyinstitute.ca/node/5061). Those were important
struggles. Unfortunately, the reality is that many of Canada’s international
crimes and interventions, like the [bombing of Libya in
2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_military_intervention_in_Libya), for
example, generated little protest by comparison.

Mark Carney is now pursuing what I would call a radical [militarist
agenda](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2026/05/27/prime-minister-
carney-announces-major-new-defence-partnership-part) and huge increases in
military spending. There’s very little organized opposition. Generally,
foreign policy issues are kind of ignored by the broader public, and there
aren’t as many institutional mechanisms for challenging them. One important
distinction between the US and Canada is that labour unions in Canada still
represent roughly [31 percent of the
workforce](https://www.fraserinstitute.org/commentary/unions-losing-ground-
canadas-private-sector), two or three times higher than the percentage in the
US. There are institutional ways for defending workers against capital.
They’re not as combative as I would like to see, and there are certainly
limitations, but those instruments do exist. When it comes to foreign policy
issues, though, it’s a very different situation. There are a few small
chapters of organizations like [World BEYOND
War](https://worldbeyondwar.org/canada/), and now Palestine has developed some
institutional infrastructure around the issue. But for the most part, anti-war
and international issues are driven by small grassroots groups that have
little money and institutional backing.

_**Daniel Falcone:** Carney might expect everyday Canadians to take peace and
reconciliation of [First Nations](https://liberal.ca/our-platform/supporting-
first-nations-priorities/) seriously domestically. Does the government’s
support for Israeli and US priorities create a [human rights credibility
gap](https://digitalcommons.schulichlaw.dal.ca/dlj/vol2/iss3/18/) and
undermine this project in your view? Further, which Canadian development
programs are rights-based, and which are corporately driven? The Liberal
approach might be to conflate them?_

**Yves Engler:** I think it would be an interesting contrast between [Carney
and Trudeau](https://itk.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Stark-contract-between-
Carney-and-Trudeau-approach-to-Indigenous-relations.pdf) on that question [of
[power sharing](https://policyoptions.irpp.org/2025/12/reconciliation-canada-
partner/)]. Trudeau had a rhetorical reconciliation agenda. I wouldn’t
necessarily call it decolonization, but there was a progressive rhetorical
element around Canada’s history of dispossession of [First
Nations](https://www.policymagazine.ca/the-carney-economic-agenda-meets-first-
nations-friction/). In practice, though, it was very limited. They didn’t even
overcome the issue of [water advisories on
reserves](https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/article/justin-trudeau-pledged-to-
end-boil-water-advisories-in-first-nations-communities-heres-how-many-are-
left/).

At one point, there were 200 or so reserves where people had to boil their
water because it wasn’t safe to drink. They did reduce that number; I think
they got it down to around 50, though I don’t remember the exact number. There
was an improvement over the seven or eight years of the Trudeau government,
but they still didn’t fully resolve [the issue](https://www.sac-
isc.gc.ca/eng/1614387410146/1614387435325). Carney, by contrast, has largely
ignored that question. In fact, he has moved quite aggressively in the
opposite direction. The so-called [Bill
C-5](https://www.wcel.org/blog/bill-c-5-building-canada-act-or-anti-democracy-
nation-dividing-act), which included the Building Canada Act, was pushed
through very early in his mandate, and it essentially reverses that
trajectory. I argue that it tramples on steps toward the principle of [free,
prior, and informed
consent](https://www.culturalsurvival.org/publications/cultural-survival-
quarterly/free-prior-and-informed-consent-protecting-indigenous) for
Indigenous First Nations when it comes to projects affecting their
territories. That has effectively been overridden by this new legislation.
Carney has taken an aggressive, openly pro-capital approach, all under the
guise of defending Canada from Trump. The whole framing is about “[building
Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/one-canadian-economy/services/building-
canada-act-projects-national-interest.html).”

Trump is destabilizing us economically, so we have this idea that we must
build more pipelines to the coast. Contradictorily, that means Indigenous
rights gets discussed but little is done. In Canada, [Indigenous
issues](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/rights-indigenous-
peoples.html) should be at the core of what is distinct about the country. But
that is not a capitalist conception. When it comes to foreign policy, I think
there is a bit of a contradiction. Rhetorically, there might be some sense
that we should have [land acknowledgement](https://chamber.ca/understanding-
land-acknowledgments-heres-what-you-need-to-know/) statements, and we should
oppose Europeans dispossessing Indigenous peoples, but then, when it comes to
Israel, that framework is completely thrown out the window. (This is the case
even among some of the [Indigenous
leadership](https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/israel-is-the-greatest-
decolonization-project-indigenous-leaders-tell-toronto-summit)).

In terms of development, there is an important dynamic in Canadian foreign
policy, which is that [aid is not really
aid](https://www.canadianaffairs.news/2026/06/24/canadas-shadow-aid-policy/)
in the way that most people think of the term. Aid is principally about
advancing Canadian geopolitical interests, and often corporate interests quite
directly. In many cases, aid is designed to advance [Canadian mining
interests](https://jacobin.com/2021/05/canada-mining-industry-justin-trudeau).
And there’s a famous example in
[Colombia](https://pbicanada.org/2021/08/21/an-overview-of-canadian-mining-
operations-in-colombia/) where Canadian aid played a central role in rewriting
the country’s [mining code](https://pbicanada.org/2021/08/21/an-overview-of-
canadian-mining-operations-in-colombia/). It rewrote it in a way that served
companies and explicitly undercut Indigenous rights.

That was a case of Canadian aid being put at the service of extractive
companies, specifically international extractive companies. And in the case of
mining, [Canada plays a dominant
role](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/adv/article-canadas-golden-
moment/). When you are talking about international mining, you are largely
talking about Canadian mining companies. There is a serious duplicitous
element to how Canadian aid projects are framed: the idea that “we’re just
trying to help the world’s poor.” But more often, these projects end up
advancing Canada’s geopolitical interests and Canadian corporate interests.

_**Daniel Falcone:** So, then Canada holds important global political
influence regarding [critical
minerals](https://canadiancriticalmineralsinc.com/) and [security issues with
the US](https://www.cfr.org/articles/canada-lays-groundwork-pivot-away-united-
states). Can its citizens develop a social movement that pushes the Carney
government to use that leverage in pursuit of peace?_

**Yves Engler:** When it comes to critical minerals, the
[Pentagon](https://transitionsecurity.org/military-minerals/) is funding
several Canadian mining projects. There was a big controversy recently around
one of these projects, which the community defeated, and the Pentagon was
funding a significant portion of it. There is this whole mechanism where the
US military is literally funding mineral projects in Canada because they are
part of this [competition with China](https://www.mining.com/web/trump-says-
us-is-announcing-a-series-of-mining-projects-worth-3-billion/) over certain
critical minerals.

Here, Canada exercises substantial leverage. It’s a wealthy country; it’s a
[member of the G7](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounders/what-does-g7-do). Could
the power of Canada as a viable State be put toward more peaceful and justice-
oriented ends? Of course it could. There’s no reason, at any theoretical
level, why it couldn’t. But the country isn’t structured in that way. [Public
opinion](https://338canada.com/) is open to a different conception of Canada,
one as a force for peace in the world. But right now, public opinion is
distracted and preoccupied with [anti-Trump
sentiment](https://www.gettyimages.ca/photos/anti-trump-protesters-in-canada).
Politically speaking, no one is saying, “Let’s pause these soldier and officer
training programs, as long as Trump is threatening to annex Canada.”

Obviously, I come at it from an internationalist and anti-imperialist angle,
but you could even frame this in a nationalist way within the political
system. The opinion polls are just overwhelming. Just like on Palestine, polls
strongly favour Palestinian rights and [Canadians reject
genocide](https://www.cjpme.org/pr_2025_08_07_poll_genocide), but it doesn’t
translate politically. Public opinion is essentially ignored. It is not
necessarily a problem of public opinion but perhaps public awareness and
political representation. If people don’t fully know what Canada has been
doing in places like [Haiti](https://jacobin.com/2024/02/canada-haiti-coup-
jean-bertrand-aristide) over the years, they won’t speak on it.

As a rule, the tendencies are not bad. Canadian tendencies are peace-minded
and internationalist. The problem is that they don’t have much [political
legitimacy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/legitimacy/) behind them, and
there isn’t really a political avenue for expressing those views. You can even
see this with something like Cuba. [Cuba](https://angusreid.org/canada-cuba-
aid/) is an interesting example because Canadian public opinion has
historically been quite different from that of the US. At the high point,
around a million Canadians were going there every year. Particularly here in
[Quebec](https://themilitant.com/2025/02/07/quebec-forum-builds-solidarity-
with-cubas-socialist-revolution/), there is a real sense of personal
connection and solidarity with Cuba. Even as many Canadians go there through
resort tourism, they still have some reference point and some level of
solidarity. [Carney](https://canadiandimension.com/articles/view/carney-wont-
support-cuba-against-us-aggression-so-we-must) has just completely capitulated
on any sense of challenging Trump’s total campaign of suffocating that
country. The government went along and [travel
advisories](https://globalnews.ca/news/11659404/air-canada-suspends-flights-
cuba-feb-2026/) were adopted by Ottawa. These measures harmed both Cuban and
Canadian companies.

Power structures are not oriented toward internationalism, justice, or
equality in international affairs. This is generally true across the board,
but it is particularly bad when it comes to foreign policy because the public
has very [little ability to
influence](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt2jcwf5) that. There are some
examples where public pressure has mattered like when the Iraq War in 2003
impacted the [Chrétien](https://www.mulroneyinstitute.ca/node/5026)
government. In the case of Iraq, Canada still supported war in a whole range
of different ways, but it didn’t provide the main thing that Bush wanted, a
formal endorsement of the coalition. And that was because of mass protests.

Other movements against apartheid in South Africa, the Vietnam War, and the
high points of peace activism and nuclear activism in the mid-to-late 1980s
were also movements that had some significant impact on Canadian policy.
Unfortunately, the victories that were won were only partial.

_**Daniel Falcone** : Some have expressed that Canada could end up as an
[American territory](https://angusreid.org/canada-51st-state-trump/) like
Puerto Rico; it is seen as a worst-case scenario. It makes it sound like the
Canadian government’s concern is less about liberation or self-determination,
and more about preserving Canada’s international power and status. Is the real
fear losing influence rather than losing sovereignty?_

******Yves Engler:** If you look at some of Carney’s first reactions to
Trump’s threats, he goes to [France and the
UK](https://www.courthousenews.com/carney-says-canada-too-reliant-on-us-on-uk-
france-trip/); he did this when we trade with Mexico. He did not prioritize or
legitimize Mexico. There’s a racial element to this just like there is a
history. The conception is, “since we are a part of NATO, we are part of the
G7, we are the big boys who help run the world.” In a narrow sense, what
Canada should be saying is “we don’t like what this current US president is
doing, and we need to be principally opposed to bad policies and commit to
those in the world struggling against domination,” to uphold long-term
Canadian legitimacy and sovereignty.
